RA lessons

These are notes from working with data for economics research projects, mainly in R and often with spatial data. They are mostly practical tips that have worked for me.

Project workflow

Work in R projects. This makes relative paths more stable. Functions like here::here() refer to files from the project root, instead of relying on whatever folder happens to be active.

Use version control. Set up git + GitHub when you create the R project (guide here). Make small commits with messages that explain the change, and use branches or pull requests when the project has several people or when a change is risky. Data files (especially heavy ones) and private files should usually go in .gitignore.

A project structure can look like:

Folder or file What goes there Notes
data/raw/ Original downloads Do not edit
data/intermediate/ Cleaned or partially constructed files Temporary datasets before joins or further manipulation
data/final/ Analysis-ready datasets
do/ 01_import, 02_clean, 03_construct, 04_analysis, etc. Use names that show the order and purpose
setup.R Packages, options, shared paths, and common functions Source it near the start of scripts that need the same setup
output/ Tables, figures, maps, reports

Set an arbitrary recorded seed. Fixed seeds are useful because they make random steps reproducible, but avoid defaults like set.seed(123) that can be copied without thought - see this blog post. One option is to choose a seed once (e.g., based on the starting date of the project), record it, and then keep using that same seed throughout the project.

AI workflow

This section will probably need updating more often than the rest.

Use skills for both reusable preferences and project-specific context. This helps when switching between projects. General instructions can be adjusted for project-specific context (e.g., if the coding style in a specific project is somewhat different than the generic one). An example structure is:

For R-specific skill files, see this guide.

ai_instructions/
  general/
    coding_style.md
    data_checks.md
    writing_style.md
  project/
    context.md
    pipeline.md
    datasets.md
File group What belongs there When it helps
General files Coding conventions, recurring checks, and writing preferences When the same preferences apply across several projects
Project files Question, unit of observation, key datasets, code structure, known edge cases etc. For most large projects
Project-specific conventions Modified versions of the general files When projects have specific rules for general preferences

Ask the AI to verify understanding. Lean prompts are often fine when the context is already clear. For tasks that are not obvious, I prefer to ask the AI to interview me briefly before implementing, or restate the task. Often, I ask it to generate a prompt, then review it and submit in a new chat.

The examples below are for simpler tasks:

Too lean More useful prompt
Make a GDP per capita map for EU countries Join EU GDP data to a map of European countries and make a choropleth by GDP per capita. Use constant US dollars. Check which countries failed to match, and whether the values look plausible.
Sum population by admin unit from the raster Extract population totals by admin unit using the population raster. Explain how partial cells are handled, confirm how missing and zero values should be treated, and inspect a few units.

Working in R

Style

I mainly use tidyverse (and dplyr) because I like its syntax and pipe-friendly style, and out of habit. Thus the examples are largely going to use it.

I often load packages with pacman::p_load, which is cleaner than many lines of library() and installs packages that are not loaded. This is convenient, but remember that it can install missing packages when the script runs.

if (!require(pacman)) install.packages('pacman', repos = 'https://cran.rstudio.com')
pacman::p_load(dplyr, labelled, sjlabelled, tidyr, ggplot2, scales, sf,
  here, readr, dtplyr, duckdb, DBI, rnaturalearth
)

options(scipen = 999)
example_df <- tibble::tibble(
  iso2 = c("US", "US", "CN", "CN"),
  gdp_t = c(25, 26, 17, 18)
)

Check package updates, for packages that you use often (e.g., dplyr), as new versions can add improved functions. However, automatic updates can be risky if an update changes the behaviour of existing functions. I also use the new pipe (|>), which is cleaner than the magrittr %>% pipe.

As an example of how coding style changes over time, see the difference between the following styles. The first one uses the old dplyr syntax and is more likely to look like AI-generated code if the AI has not been told otherwise:

example_df %>% 
  group_by(iso2) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_gdp = mean(gdp_t)
    ) %>%
  ungroup()

Or, a bit cleaner:

example_df |> 
  summarise(
    avg_gdp = mean(gdp_t),
    .by = iso2
    )

Speed

dplyr is rather fast for most operations. For most of my work, the difference was not large enough to matter. Still, there are faster alternatives:

Tool What it is When to use
data.table A fast alternative syntax for data work If you prefer its syntax and need better performance
dtplyr A dplyr front end that translates to data.table If you want dplyr syntax with some data.table speed
duckdb An in-process SQL database When the data is too large to comfortably keep in memory

An example:

set.seed(23072026) # date of project start

speed_df <- tibble::tibble(
  iso2 = sample(sprintf("C%03d", 1:200), 3000000, replace = TRUE),
  year = sample(2000:2024, 3000000, replace = TRUE),
  gdp_t = runif(3000000, 1, 100),
  pop_m = runif(3000000, 1, 1500)
)

dplyr_elapsed <- system.time({
  dplyr_result <- speed_df |>
    mutate(
      gdp_pc = gdp_t * 1000000 / pop_m,
      large = gdp_t > 50
    ) |>
    filter(large, year >= 2010) |>
    summarise(
      avg_gdp_pc = mean(gdp_pc),
      total_gdp = sum(gdp_t),
      n = n(),
      .by = c(iso2, year)
      )
})[["elapsed"]]

cat("dplyr elapsed:", round(dplyr_elapsed, 3), "seconds\n")
## dplyr elapsed: 0.63 seconds
dtplyr_elapsed <- system.time({
  dtplyr_result <- speed_df |>
    lazy_dt() |>
    mutate(
      gdp_pc = gdp_t * 1000000 / pop_m,
      large = gdp_t > 50
    ) |>
    filter(large, year >= 2010) |>
    summarise(
      avg_gdp_pc = mean(gdp_pc),
      total_gdp = sum(gdp_t),
      n = n(),
      .by = c(iso2, year)
      ) |>
    as_tibble()
})[["elapsed"]]

cat("dtplyr elapsed:", round(dtplyr_elapsed, 3), "seconds\n")
## dtplyr elapsed: 0.42 seconds
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())
duckdb_register(con, "speed_df", speed_df)

duckdb_elapsed <- system.time({
  duckdb_result <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "
    SELECT
      iso2,
      year,
      AVG(gdp_t * 1000000 / pop_m) AS avg_gdp_pc,
      SUM(gdp_t) AS total_gdp,
      COUNT(*) AS n
    FROM speed_df
    WHERE gdp_t > 50
      AND year >= 2010
    GROUP BY iso2, year
    "
  )
})[["elapsed"]]

cat("duckdb elapsed:", round(duckdb_elapsed, 3), "seconds\n")
## duckdb elapsed: 0.09 seconds
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)

For many operations, the difference is very small, and the setup cost might take longer than the calculation.

Functions with the same names

Some R functions from different packages have identical names, which can create bugs that may be hard to spot. For example, take the lag function. stats::lag can produce confusing results, while it might be the default lag. dplyr::lag (or data.table::shift(type = "lag")) are clearer and more reliable.

lag_example <- tibble::tibble(
  year = 2020:2022,
  gdp = c(100, 120, 140)
)

lag_example |>
  mutate(
    `dplyr::lag` = dplyr::lag(gdp),
    `stats::lag` = as.numeric(stats::lag(gdp))
  )
## # A tibble: 3 × 4
##    year   gdp `dplyr::lag` `stats::lag`
##   <int> <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>
## 1  2020   100           NA          100
## 2  2021   120          100          120
## 3  2022   140          120          140

Similarly, if code uses select without specifying dplyr::select, and raster has also been loaded, the code might call raster::select instead (at least that tends to break with a warning).

Another example is copy_labels, which exists in both sjlabelled and labelled. The two versions do not use the same argument order, and they may change values while copying labels, so in those cases write the package name explicitly (ideally in the setup file) and check the documentation.

Data construction

Working with country-level data

A lot of the analysis I have done is at the country level. Much of this analysis is similar when using other units of analysis.

Country identifiers

Use ISO codes rather than names. Country names work well in plots and tables, but they are often inconsistent across datasets. For example, “Ivory Coast” and “Cote d’Ivoire” may refer to the same country. Thus, I prefer to use ISO codes (e.g., CIV). However, ISO codes also have limitations: South Sudan’s ISO3 may appear as SSD in one source and SDS in another; Namibia’s ISO2 code is NA, which can be read as missing data; and aggregates, disputed areas, territories, and historical countries can create other problems.

For illustration, I use WDI population and constant-dollar GDP files, and want to keep all countries. I convert the ISO3 codes to ISO2 with the countrycode package, then inspect the rows that failed conversion.

Most failed conversions are aggregates, such as regions and income, but there is also a country that fails the conversion - Kosovo, which is seemingly not mapped in countrycode. Thus, I map it manually:

Raw label ISO3 ISO2 conversion Decision Why
United States USA US keep ordinary country
Kosovo XKX failed manual code XK special case
Low income LIC failed drop aggregate 
country_panel <- country_panel_all |> 
  mutate(
    iso2 = if_else(iso3 == "XKX", "XK", iso2)
  ) |> 
  filter_out(is.na(iso2)) # filter_out is a new dplyr function

Geographic consistency over time

Geographic units do not always keep the same boundaries over time. Countries change borders, gain independence, or split; this is also true for administrative units. Various datasets handle those changes differently. A value in a given year might refer to current borders, old borders, or something in between. For country-level data, pay attention to disputed territories and places whose borders changed around the period of analysis. Sudan might mean present-day Sudan, or also include South Sudan. Kosovo - if it even appears in the data - might be under the rows of Yugoslavia (until 2003), Serbia and Montenegro (2003-2006), Serbia (2006-2008), or as Kosovo (generally 2008-, but in various datasets might appear as independent only from a later year). Taiwan and Palestine can also be coded or named in different ways depending on the source. Check the metadata to verify those cases.

Join keys, merge types, and row multiplication

Quite often we need to join datasets using one or more common keys. My default is to work with a master dataset that includes the units used in the final analysis, and then add variables to it with left_join(). I use the other joins mostly for filtering and diagnostics:

Join What it does When I use it
left_join() Keeps master rows and adds variables Main construction
inner_join() Keeps rows that match in both datasets Filtering
anti_join() Finds rows that do not match Diagnostics
full_join() Keeps rows from both datasets Coverage checks
semi_join() Keeps master rows with a match Occasional filtering
right_join() Keeps rows from the added dataset Rarely

I mainly use the first three in ordinary construction scripts.

For example:

Master data
ISO3 Region
USA North America
CHN East Asia
IND South Asia
MEX Latin America
Added GDP data
ISO3 GDP (bn)
USA 23000
CHN 18000
IND 3500
DEU 4200
left_join()

Keeps the master rows. Mexico stays, but GDP is missing

USACHNINDMEX
MEX keeps its region, but GDP is missing; DEU is not added
inner_join()

Keeps only rows that match in both files

USACHNIND
MEX and DEU are both excluded
full_join()

Keeps everything from both files. Good for checking coverage

USACHNINDMEXDEU
MEX has missing GDP; DEU has missing region

Before joining, check the unit of observation, key uniqueness, unmatched rows, and missing values created by the join. Also look for accidental duplicate columns like country_name.x and country_name.y.

Variable construction

Once the rows and keys are under control, the next problems are definitions, labels, units, missing values, aggregation rules, and derived variables.

Definitions, units, and derived variables

Pay attention to definitions and units. For example, gdp could mean nominal GDP in current local currency, nominal GDP in current USD, real GDP in constant USD, or PPP-adjusted GDP.

Even after the source and units are clear, small changes in the formula can create different variables. Total GDP, GDP per person, logged GDP, and logged GDP per person are not interchangeable.

Aggregation rules and aggregate units

Notice what the aggregates contain and their names. In some datasets there may be aggregates (e.g., “Middle East” in a country-level dataset). Some datasets have variables that identify them, but not always, and the names of aggregate countries can differ across datasets. In FAOSTAT, one dataset has an aggregate called “Low Income Food Deficit Countries”, while another uses “Low Income Food Deficit Countries (LIFDCs)”. Since there is not always an ISO2/3 equivalent for each aggregate, pay attention to those cases.

Missing values

Missing values can mean different things - the value was not collected, it was not applicable, it was withheld or hidden for privacy or reliability reasons, it failed to merge, or it is unknown. R will often show these as NA, but there are some variants - NaN is the result of an undefined numeric operation, such as 0 / 0, while NULL usually means that the object is absent.

Missing values need an explicit rule. During construction, first try to understand why they are missing. Then decide whether to leave them as missing or replace them using a documented rule justified by the project. Suppose that NAs mean missingness, and we want to sum GDP over 2023-2025 for each country:

Country 2023 2024 2025
Bolivia 42.1 43.0 NA
Cuba NA NA NA
Eritrea 2.3 NA 2.5

The main choices are:

na.rm = TRUE

Use the observed values. For sums, an all-missing country returns 0, which may be misleading

na.rm = FALSE

Return NA if any value is missing. This is strict, but can erase usable partial information.

NA only if all missing

Use observed values when at least one exists, but keep fully missing countries as missing

Country Observed years Sum rule
na.rm = TRUE na.rm = FALSE NA only if all missing
Bolivia 2 of 3 85.1 NA 85.1
Cuba 0 of 3 0.0 NA NA
Eritrea 2 of 3 4.8 NA 4.8

Choose the rule explicitly, and show the amount of missingness next to the aggregate if relevant:

df |>
  summarise(
    total = if (all(is.na(x))) NA_real_ else sum(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_observed = sum(!is.na(x)),
    .by = group
  )

Validation

Run checks after important construction steps. Joins, aggregations, spatial matches, and output construction are examples. The exact check depends on the operation, but the goal is the same: make silent mistakes visible early. A lot of results will look odd; sometimes it is easier to catch problems during construction, although some only become visible when you see the final results and suspect that something is off.

Messages and quick checks

Add short messages after certain construction steps, to make mistakes easier to notice. This can make the code harder to read, but it has some value when used sparingly, especially since code is increasingly read by AI tools. For example:

joined_country_regions <- country_regions |>
  left_join(
    country_gdp |> 
      select(-country_name),
    join_by(iso3)
  )

unmatched_country_regions <- country_regions |>
  filter_out(iso3 %in% country_gdp$iso3)

message(
  n_distinct(country_regions$iso3) - nrow(unmatched_country_regions), " of ",
  n_distinct(country_regions$iso3), " country-region units matched to GDP."
)
## 3 of 4 country-region units matched to GDP.
message(
  nrow(unmatched_country_regions), " country-region units did not match to GDP."
)
## 1 country-region units did not match to GDP.
message(
  sum(is.na(joined_country_regions$gdp_b)), " rows have missing GDP after the join."
)
## 1 rows have missing GDP after the join.

Checks after risky steps

After this step Quick check Message
Join Expected unit of observation; row counts before and after; unmatched keys; missingness in new variables 247 of 250 country-year rows matched; 3 unmatched ISO3 codes.
Aggregation Rows collapsed per group; groups with all missing inputs; unexpected zeros or extreme totals Collapsed 12,500 rows to 250 groups; 4 groups have all-missing GDP.
Spatial match Unmatched points or polygons; multiple matches; a quick map of matched and unmatched units 98.6% of points matched to an admin unit; 42 points unmatched.
Output construction Expected file exists; row count, column count, CRS, and key variables are present Wrote final_country_panel.rds with 5,250 rows and 37 columns.

Plots

Plots in economic research have two main jobs. First, inspecting the data. These plots can be simple because the goal is to understand the data and detect issues, such as implausible or missing values. Second, presenting the results and sharing the main insights. These plots should be clean, concise, and should reduce the effort required from the reader.

Some tips that often help:

  • remove axis titles when the title already says what is plotted, when their meaning is implied (years), or when they are hard to read (most y-axes)
  • directly label a few important series instead of using a legend
  • grey out background series when the figure focuses on few important series
  • name a specific visualization guide when asking AI for plot suggestions, rather than asking for a “better plot” in general
  • add annotations when they clarify the figure, although they are annoying to code in R

There are better guides than this. I really like Saloni Dattani’s guide. The R Graph Gallery is also a nice source for examples.

The graph type should follow the question. This is a very partial list, but some examples:
Graph type Best for Note
Line Changes over time Good when order matters
Bar Comparing categories Can work well if there aren’t many categories
Stacked bar/area Composition or totals Can be hard to read
Pie Rarely Avoid in most cases - shares are hard to read
Scatter Relationships between two variables Good when order does not matter
Histogram/density Distributions Good for highlighting skew, outliers and bunching

The next plots show the same data moving from a quick inspection graph to a cleaner presentation version.

A very basic version of a plot is:

plot_df |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_line(aes(x = year, y = gdp_pc, color = iso2)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2024, 4), limits = c(2000, 2024)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), labels = label_dollar()) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(title = "GDP per capita across EU countries")

Notice that the axis titles are unnecessary (‘gdp_pc’ is implied from the title, ‘year’ is easily understood); and that it’s extremely hard to understand which line refers to which country.

Suppose we want to focus on Ireland’s rise from Sweden’s level of GDP per capita to nearly Luxembourg’s. We can highlight those countries and keep the other EU countries in grey, and remove the axis titles and legend:

plot_colors <- c(
  "IE" = "#0072B2",
  "LU" = "#D55E00",
  "SE" = "#009E73",
  "Other countries" = "#b8bec6"
)

line_labels <- plot_df |> 
  filter(iso2 %in% highlight_countries) |> 
  summarise(
    gdp_pc = gdp_pc[which.max(year)],
    year = max(year),
    label = country_name[which.max(year)],
    .by = iso2
  )

plot_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = gdp_pc, group = iso2)) + 
  geom_line(aes(color = highlighted), linewidth = 0.9, alpha = 0.85) + 
  geom_text(
    data = line_labels,
    aes(label = iso2, color = iso2),
    hjust = 0,
    nudge_x = 0.25,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = plot_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2024, 4), limits = c(2000, 2025.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), labels = label_dollar()) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.margin = margin(5.5, 60, 5.5, 5.5)
  ) + 
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "GDP per capita in Ireland compared to the rest of the EU")

That is already easier to read than many default plots. A more polished version can use a cleaner background, an informative title and subtitle, and country names instead of raw codes:

plot_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = gdp_pc, group = iso2)) + 
  geom_line(aes(color = highlighted), linewidth = 0.9, alpha = 0.8) + 
  geom_text(
    data = line_labels,
    aes(label = label, color = iso2),
    hjust = 0,
    nudge_x = 0.25,
    fontface = "bold",
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = plot_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2000, 2024, 4), limits = c(2000, 2025.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Ireland spiked toward the EU's richest",
    subtitle = "GDP per capita, constant 2015 US dollars",
    caption = "Source: The World Bank"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f7f8f3", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#f7f8f3", color = NA),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "#6b7280"),
    plot.margin = margin(5.5, 50, 5.5, 5.5)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off")

Spatial data basics

There are two main types of spatial datasets:
Type What it stores Common examples R package
Vector Points, lines, or polygons Boundaries, roads, locations sf
Raster Values in grid cells Climate, elevation, population terra

For vector data in R, use sf. Most of the time, sf::read_sf() and sf::write_sf() are convenient wrappers around st_read() and st_write(), unless a file has many layers. Vector data is often saved as shapefiles. Shapefiles are split across several files (.shp, .shx, .dbf, etc.) and have short column-name limits. Use geopackages (.gpkg) when possible. They are more efficient and easier to work with.

For raster data in R, use terra. Raster data is often saved as .tif, especially for ordinary gridded layers. Another common format is .nc or NetCDF, which is often used for climate data.

Pay attention to CRS and projections. A CRS tells R how coordinates on the screen relate to places on Earth. Areas, distances, buffers, and centroids can be misleading if the data are in longitude/latitude or if layers use different CRS, so check st_crs()/crs() and use st_transform when needed to a projection that makes sense for the operation.

Which tool to use

Tool Examples Main advantages Main drawbacks
Programming languages R, Python Reproducible; easy to combine with cleaning and modeling Storage, memory, and visual inspection
GIS software QGIS, ArcGIS Visual inspection, manual exploration, cartography Less convenient for scripted workflows
Google Earth Engine Code Editor, Python API Hosted catalogs and large raster summaries Quotas and server-side debugging

Several notes on GIS software and GEE:

  • ArcGIS is powerful but not free
  • You can also program inside GIS tools, but I find that less convenient than sf in R
  • GEE is best when the data already exists in the Earth Engine data catalog or the GEE community catalog - such as Hansen forest loss data or GHSL built-up - as you avoid downloading and storing large rasters
  • The coding experience in GEE is more annoying, but there’s now a Gemini assistant there (which requires a Gemini API key, so is not unlimited).
  • GEE’s new quotas still allow rather comfortably to get spatial aggregations and so on, but more limited for heavier operations like geometric operations or raw image analysis
  • For GEE, using the Python API can keep the spatial step in the same project workflow, but it’s harder to visually debug; you can start in the GEE code editor and let an AI convert it to Python when done (verify that outputs are identical)

When unsure, AI can help consider the trade-offs. Since trying a small R version is now cheap, start there and check whether it is fast enough.

Recommendations for working with GEE

  • If the same spatial units appear in several scripts, create one master feature collection, such as var worldUnits = ee.FeatureCollection('projects/ee-your_project/assets/worldUnits');. Then each script can call the same cleaned units.
  • If AI suggests a boundary dataset such as FAO/GAUL/2015/level0, check whether territories or administrative units need to be merged before grouping by ISO3. Country-level comparisons can be wrong if the boundary file uses different units.
  • If the boundary file needs cleaning, use a separate GEE script to clean names, match to ISO3, merge units, and export a reusable asset. Analysis scripts stay shorter and call the same version of the cleaned boundary file.

Spatial matching

Spatial units often require join operations, and those joins require judgment calls. A unit may intersect several polygons, a point may fall just outside a boundary because the datasets use slightly different borders, or a raster cell may only partly overlap the polygon. We have several options, such as:
Type Usual pattern Risk Immediate check
Point to polygon st_join(…, st_within) Unmatched points; duplicate matches Count unmatched and multiply matched points
Polygon overlap st_intersection() Rows multiply; area can be wrong Check row counts and overlap shares
Nearest match st_nearest_feature() or nngeo::st_nn() A nearest feature can still be far away Store distance and flag matches above a cutoff
Raster extraction terra::extract() Partial cells; wrong aggregation Check weights and compare a few polygons

If the polygons in one source can overlap each other, decide whether those overlaps should count once or several times before intersecting them with the units of analysis.

For example, overlay the Netherlands and Belgium with a 0.5 by 0.5 degree grid. Some grid cells cross the border. We can use st_intersection() to calculate the share of each cell that lies within each country:

country_grid_overlap <- st_intersection(country_grid, countries) |>
  mutate(overlap_area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(st_transform(geometry, 3035))) / 1e6)

Maps

For maps in R, ggplot2 with geom_sf() is often enough. A choropleth map needs two inputs: boundaries and a variable to color each area.

This example first highlights a bug. If we join by ISO2, France is not matched because the rnaturalearth file uses -99 as its ISO2 code (as France has several territories).

eu_gdp_2024 <- country_panel |>
  filter(year == 2024, iso2 %in% eu27_countries) |>
  mutate(gdp_pc = gdp_b * 1000 / pop_m) |>
  select(iso2, iso3, gdp_pc)

europe_boundaries <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(
  scale = "small",
  returnclass = "sf"
) |> 
  select(iso2 = iso_a2, iso3 = adm0_a3, continent, geometry) |>
  filter(continent == "Europe")

iso2_join_diagnostic <- europe_boundaries |>
  mutate(in_eu = iso2 %in% eu27_countries) |>
  left_join(
    eu_gdp_2024 |> select(iso2, gdp_pc),
    join_by(iso2)
  )

iso2_join_diagnostic |>
  filter(iso3 %in% c("FRA", "DEU", "ESP")) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(iso2_boundary = iso2, iso3, in_eu, gdp_pc)
##   iso2_boundary iso3 in_eu   gdp_pc
## 1           -99  FRA FALSE       NA
## 2            DE  DEU  TRUE 44027.55
## 3            ES  ESP  TRUE 29245.12
iso2_join_diagnostic |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(fill = "#d9d9d9", color = "white", linewidth = 0.12) +
  geom_sf(
    data = iso2_join_diagnostic |> filter(in_eu),
    aes(fill = gdp_pc),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.12
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    labels = label_number(scale = 1 / 1000, suffix = "k"),
    na.value = "#eeeeee",
    guide = guide_colorbar(
      title = NULL,
      barwidth = grid::unit(160, "pt"),
      barheight = grid::unit(8, "pt"),
      label.position = "bottom"
    )
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-12, 35), ylim = c(34, 72), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "#6b7280")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "GDP per capita across EU countries",
    subtitle = "Reveals a bad join: France is not merged",
    caption = "Source: The World Bank"
  )

The fix is to join by ISO3 in this case. For presentation, the scale depends on the comparison: continuous color, or binned values; and if binned, which bins? The first version keeps a wide top category, which is excellent for distinguishing between the richest (Luxembourg and Ireland), the relatively rich (Germany, Sweden), the ‘somewhat’ rich (Spain, Italy) and the relatively poorer countries of the EU (Poland, Bulgaria). The second version uses the same palette but compresses the top and gives more detail in the middle and bottom, making it easier to distinguish between for example Poland and Bulgaria:

eu_gdp_map <- europe_boundaries |>
  mutate(in_eu = iso3 %in% eu_gdp_2024$iso3) |>
  left_join(
    eu_gdp_2024 |> select(iso3, gdp_pc),
    join_by(iso3)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    gdp_pc_group_wide = cut(
      gdp_pc,
      breaks = c(0, 20000, 35000, 50000, 70000, Inf),
      labels = c("<$20k", "$20k-$35k", "$35k-$50k", "$50k-$70k", "$70k+"),
      right = FALSE
    ),
    gdp_pc_group_middle = cut(
      gdp_pc,
      breaks = c(0, 10000, 15000, 20000, 30000, 40000, Inf),
      labels = c("<$10k", "$10k-$15k", "$15k-$20k", "$20k-$30k", "$30k-$40k", "$40k+"),
      right = FALSE
    )
  )

eu_gdp_map |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(fill = "#d9d9d9", color = "white", linewidth = 0.12) +
  geom_sf(
    data = eu_gdp_map |> filter(in_eu),
    aes(fill = gdp_pc_group_wide),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.12
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "<$20k" = "#edf8fb",
      "$20k-$35k" = "#b2e2e2",
      "$35k-$50k" = "#66c2a4",
      "$50k-$70k" = "#2ca25f",
      "$70k+" = "#006d2c"
    ),
    na.value = "#eeeeee",
    name = NULL
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-12, 35), ylim = c(34, 72), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "#6b7280")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Wide bins separate the richest countries",
    caption = "Source: The World Bank"
  )

eu_gdp_map |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(fill = "#d9d9d9", color = "white", linewidth = 0.12) +
  geom_sf(
    data = eu_gdp_map |> filter(in_eu),
    aes(fill = gdp_pc_group_middle),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.12
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "<$10k" = "#edf8fb",
      "$10k-$15k" = "#ccece6",
      "$15k-$20k" = "#99d8c9",
      "$20k-$30k" = "#66c2a4",
      "$30k-$40k" = "#2ca25f",
      "$40k+" = "#006d2c"
    ),
    na.value = "#eeeeee",
    name = NULL
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-12, 35), ylim = c(34, 72), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "#6b7280")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Narrower bins show more middle and lower variation",
    caption = "Source: The World Bank"
  )

Representative points of polygons

Sometimes we want to use one point for a unit rather than the full polygon. That is especially common when the analysis is heavy, for example calculating road paths between units, or when the question is about specific places inside the unit.

Which point should we use? It depends on what the point is meant to represent:

Question Point choice Check before using it
Where is the geometric center of this unit? Centroid Does it fall outside the polygon or in a useless empty area?
I need a point inside the polygon st_point_on_surface() Is the point substantively reasonable, not just technically inside?
Where is the average person in this unit? Population-weighted centroid Does the point fall between population centers or outside the unit?
What is the main populated place? Highest-population cell or main city Is the raster/city source at the right resolution for the project?
